plain: ElevenLabs turns text into spoken audio that doesn't sound like a robot: you paste a script, pick a voice, and it hands you back an audio file. It does three things that genuinely matter: reading a text with a catalog voice, cloning a voice (yours, with your permission) so it can read anything, and dubbing a video into another language while keeping the original voice. It's used for video voiceovers, training audio, voicemail greetings, podcasts, and accessibility. The honest comparison: it's an extremely fast, cheap narrator who doesn't understand what they're reading, so the intonation of an ironic line or a figure is something you have to direct yourself.

account.free: It's measured in characters, not minutes: every letter you send counts. The free plan gave about 10,000 characters a month as of August 2026, which is about ten minutes of audio, and does NOT allow commercial use or remove attribution. Paid plans started around 5 dollars a month and go up based on characters. Before using an audio clip for something you're being paid for, check two things on the plans page: that your plan allows commercial use and that it gives you rights over what's generated. Check it yourself at elevenlabs.io: plans change.
steps: Go to elevenlabs.io and sign up
Google is the fastest way. You'll see a panel with a big text box and a list of voices on the right.
Try a catalog voice before anything else
Paste two real sentences of your own, not «hello, this is a test». Listen to three or four different voices with the SAME text: it's the only way to compare.

There are voices in different English accents (US, UK, Australian...), and they don't sound the same or work for the same things. Filter by language before falling in love with a voice that'll later sing off-key.
In your profile. Note how many you have left for the month. A two-minute video script is about 1,800 characters: do the math before generating twenty versions.
If you're going to clone a voice, start with your own
You need a clean recording a few minutes long, no music or background noise. And you need explicit permission if the voice isn't yours: the platform will make you confirm it, and it means it.
Check commercial use before you invoice
It's on the plans page. If the audio is going into a client's video, check this before accepting the job.
account.warning: Cloning someone else's voice without their explicit, written permission isn't a prank: it's a serious legal problem, and it's worse with a well-known person's voice. In many places a person's voice is legally protected as part of their identity. If the project calls for it, get signed permission before uploading a single audio file.

first: Paste a real text of yours, about five lines, and listen to it with three different voices before deciding.
Change only the stability setting and regenerate the same text: you'll instantly understand what that control does.
Write a figure and a time in the script and listen to it: you'll see how it reads them, which is almost never how you expect.
Try placing commas and periods where you want it to breathe. Punctuation is your directing tool.
Download the audio in the best quality and listen to it on your phone's speaker, which is how most people will hear it.
shortcuts: Stability

The control that changes the result the most. Low: the voice has more emotion and more surprises; high: it's flatter and more predictable. For video voiceover, raise it; for something with life, lower it. Test with the same text.
Similarity
How closely it sticks to the original voice. Very high can drag along flaws from the source recording: if it comes out with weird noise, lower this first.
Style / exaggeration
How much interpretation it adds. Raising it a lot sounds theatrical and increases mistakes. For an informational script, keep it low.
Punctuation as direction
Commas are short pauses, periods are long pauses, ellipses are hesitation. It's the most reliable way to direct intonation, far more than the settings.
Writing numbers out as words
«twelve hundred dollars» reads well; «$1,200» is a lottery. Same with times, dates, and abbreviations: write them exactly how you want them to sound.
The seed / regenerating
Every generation is different. If you like a take, download it right then: you might not get it exactly the same again.
Voice cloning
Uploading recordings to create a new voice. Needs clean audio and permission. The clone's quality depends almost entirely on the quality of what you upload.
Dubbing
Takes a video and turns it into another language while keeping the timbre of the original voice. Always review it: it translates well on average and fails on proper names and technical terms.
Projects
For long texts: a chapter, a course, an audiobook. Lets you work in pieces and change one section's voice without regenerating everything.
The character counter
Check it before a long session. Twenty versions of a two-minute script is forty thousand characters: four months of the free plan.
daily: Write the script for the ear, not the eye. Short sentences. What looks elegant in text sounds convoluted read aloud. Read it yourself out loud before generating it: wherever you stumble, the voice will too.
Write numbers, times, and abbreviations exactly how you want them to sound. It's the setting that solves the most problems and isn't in any menu.
Compare voices with the same text, not different texts. It's the only comparison that's valid.
Download every take you like right away. Generations don't repeat exactly, and losing a good one by not saving it is a classic mistake.
Count characters before you start. It's this tool's currency and it gets spent much faster than it seems when you're trying out versions.
Check commercial use and rights before invoicing. Same as with video: check before accepting the job, not after delivering it.

templates.name: The voiceover script prepared to sound good
templates.what: A text written for the eye sounds odd read aloud. This template turns a normal script into one prepared for a synthetic voice: numbers spelled out, pauses marked with punctuation, and short sentences. Works for videos, training, and recorded messages.
templates.how: 1) Write the normal script first. 2) Read it aloud yourself: wherever you stumble, cut the sentence. 3) Convert numbers, times, and abbreviations into words. 4) Mark pauses with punctuation, not with instructions in parentheses (it doesn't understand those). 5) Generate it, listen to the whole thing, and fix only what sounds off.
fill: If you can't say a sentence in one breath, neither can the voice
«twelve hundred» not «1,200». Same with times and dates
Write out how they're pronounced: «V-A-T», spell it out if you want it letter by letter
Comma = short pause. Period = long pause. New paragraph = a breath
templates.code:
─── BEFORE (written to be read) ───────────────────────────
Our service, which has been running since 2019 and is
already used by more than 1,200 companies across the country,
cuts management time by up to 40% (according to internal data).

─── AFTER (written to be heard) ───────────────────────────
Our service has been running since two thousand nineteen.

More than twelve hundred companies across the country use it.

And it cuts management time by up to forty percent.

─── RULES ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. One idea per sentence.
2. No parentheses and no asides: the voice doesn't mark them.
3. Numbers, times, dates, and percentages, spelled out.
4. Abbreviations, written the way they sound.
5. A new paragraph wherever you want it to breathe.
6. No sentence longer than twenty words.

errors: It misreads numbers, times, or abbreviations

It's not its fault: it can't know whether «1,200» is twelve hundred or one point two. Write it out exactly the way you want to hear it. It's the fix for half of all voiceover problems and it's not in any setting.
The voice sounds noisy, metallic, or with strange echoes

If it's a cloned voice, the problem is in the audio you uploaded: background noise, music, or a bad microphone. Lower the similarity setting, which is what drags along the original's flaws, and if that doesn't help, re-record the sample in a quiet room.
It sounds different every time I generate

That's normal: every generation is a new take, like in a studio. That's why the rule is to download the good take right away. For a long text, use project mode and lock in the pieces that are already good.
I ran out of characters mid-month

They get spent much faster than it seems when you're trying out versions. Before generating the whole script, test settings with a thirty-word paragraph, and only once they're decided, generate everything. That saves 80% of your usage.
The intonation has no emotion, sounds flat

Raise style and lower stability, and test with the same text to compare. But first check the script: a long, subordinate-clause-heavy sentence sounds flat no matter who reads it. Short sentences give more rhythm than any setting.
The dubbing mistranslates proper names or technical terms
This happens with every automated system. Always review the transcript before generating the dub: most tools let you correct the intermediate text, and that's where names get fixed.
I can't use the audio commercially
The free plan doesn't allow it and also requires attribution. Fixed by upgrading the plan, and checked before accepting a client job, not after delivering it.

prompts.name: Turn a text into a script that reads well aloud
prompts.prompt: I'm going to paste you a text and I want you to turn it into a voiceover script ready for a synthetic voice. Don't summarize it or change its meaning: adapt it for the ear. Do this. One: break up long sentences so none goes over twenty words and each carries a single idea. Two: convert every number, percentage, time, date, amount, and abbreviation into words, written exactly how I want them to sound. Three: remove parentheses and asides, which don't get marked in speech: if the information matters, turn it into its own sentence, and if not, cut it. Four: place punctuation with pauses in mind: comma for a short pause, period for a long pause, new paragraph wherever it should breathe. Five: flag with a margin note the three or four sentences where the intonation is going to be tricky, and tell me how you'd rewrite them if they sound off. Six: tell me how many characters the final script has, so I know what I'll spend. Seven: at the end, give me the clean text ready to paste, without your notes. The text is: [PASTE IT]. It's for: [A VIDEO / TRAINING AUDIO / A VOICEMAIL GREETING] and should ideally run: [HOW LONG].

prompts.name: Choose a voice and settings for what I need
prompts.prompt: I need to decide which voice and which settings to use in ElevenLabs and I don't know where to start. Help me with a method, not a blind recommendation. One: ask me what the audio is for, who's going to listen to it, in what context they'll listen (headphones, a phone speaker, a video with music behind it) and what feeling I want to convey. Two: tell me what voice traits suit me (low or high pitch, pacing, which accent) and why, based on my answers. Three: tell me what values to start with for stability, similarity, and style, and explain in one sentence what each one does, so I can adjust them myself. Four: give me a thirty-word test text, specific to my case, that works for comparing voices against each other: it has to include a figure, a proper name, and a line with emotion, which is where the differences show. Five: tell me what to pay attention to while listening in order to decide, because they'll all sound good the first time. Six: remind me what to check in my plan if this is going into paid work. My case is: [DESCRIBE IT].

words: Character
The billing unit. Every letter in the script counts, spaces included. A minute of audio is about 900.
Stability
How restrained the voice is. High: flat and predictable. Low: more emotion and more surprises.
Similarity
How closely a clone sticks to the original voice. Very high also drags along the recording's flaws.
Voice cloning
Creating a new voice from recordings. Needs clean audio and the person's permission.
Dubbing
Turning a video into another language while keeping the original voice's timbre.
Take
Each generation. Like in a studio: no two are alike, so the good one gets downloaded right away.
Project
The mode for long texts, letting you work in pieces without regenerating everything.
Commercial use
Whether your plan lets you use the audio for something you're paid for. Checked before accepting the job.
Attribution
The requirement to say what the audio was made with. The free plan requires it.
Script for the ear
A text written to be heard: short sentences, numbers spelled out, no asides.
matters: Writing numbers, times, and abbreviations out as words. Solves half of all voiceover problems and doesn't appear in any settings menu.
Testing settings with a short paragraph before generating the whole script. It's what separates spending a thousand characters from spending forty thousand.
Downloading every good take right away. They don't repeat exactly, and losing a good one by not saving it happens once and is never forgotten.
Written permission before cloning anyone's voice. A person's voice is legally protected and this doesn't allow shortcuts.
ignore: Fine-tuning settings while the script isn't well written yet. A text written badly for the ear sounds bad with any voice and any configuration.
Trying twenty different voices. Pick three that fit the job, compare them with the same text, and decide. Beyond that is indecision, not judgment.
Voice cloning on your first jobs. Catalog voices are excellent and don't drag you into the permissions issue.
